topic: Churn Starts Before Cancellation: The Member Signals Studios May Be Missing

facts.label: Story
facts.value: Churn Starts Before Cancellation: The Member Signals Studios May Be Missing

facts.label: Article
facts.value: Mariana Tek data shows the warning signs of member churn can appear months in advance, giving studios more time to recognize changing behavior and strengthen engagement. A member can be disengaging long before a studio has any obvious reason to think they’re at risk of leaving. The decision to cancel or downgrade may be developing for months. New data from Mariana Tek shows measurable changes in member behavior three to eight months before a cancellation or downgrade, which suggests studios may have a much larger window to recognize disengagement and respond. “The membership change is often the end of a slow, subtle disengagement trajectory, not the beginning of one,” said Julie Sippy, director of marketing at Mariana Tek. That trajectory can be difficult to spot because disengaged members don’t necessarily disappear. They may still attend classes, generate revenue and appear as active members in a studio’s system. What changes is the pattern. According to the data, for members who eventually canceled, average monthly visits fell from 6.2 three months before cancellation to 5.4 in the final month, while monthly spend declined 11%. The pattern becomes even more pronounced among some members who downgrade their memberships.

topic: The Invisible Layer: Electromagnetic Exposure and Human Health in the Built Environment

facts.label: Story
facts.value: The Invisible Layer: Electromagnetic Exposure and Human Health in the Built Environment

facts.label: Article
facts.value: We’ve learned to recognize what makes a space feel good. Natural light, fresh air, materiality, and connection to nature have become essential ingredients in how we shape healthier environments. These elements are now widely understood, measured, and intentionally designed. Alongside them, another layer is present in almost every space we inhabit, quiet, unseen, and rarely part of the design conversation: electromagnetic fields (EMFs). They are embedded in the infrastructure of modern life, supporting connectivity, communication, and the systems we rely on daily. Their presence is constant, forming part of the environmental background of contemporary living. As time spent indoors and connected continues to increase, so does the relevance of understanding how these conditions interact with the body. The human body operates through finely tuned electrical processes. Neural communication, cardiac rhythms, and cellular activity all rely on bioelectrical signaling. Within this context, the environments we occupy become part of a continuous exchange with our physiology. Research compiled by the Building Biology Institute points to associations between elevated electromagnetic exposure and changes in sleep patterns, nervous system activity, cognitive fatigue, and hormonal regulation, particularly melatonin. Melatonin plays a central role in circadian rhythms and cellular repair.

en.headline: The Invisible Layer: Electromagnetic Exposure and Human Health in the Built Environment

topic: Fitness community raises £3,330 in pink challenge

facts.label: Story
facts.value: Fitness community raises £3,330 in pink challenge

facts.label: Article
facts.value: J Potter Community Fitness raised £3,330 for Breast Cancer Now after supporters walked, danced and exercised their way through a 776-mile challenge. 0 Comments Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share The Big Pink Journey, organised by J Potter Community Fitness, raised £3,330 for Breast Cancer Now through a collective effort that saw supporters travel 776 miles in just one week. The original fundraising target was £1,500, and the distance goal was 315 miles—the equivalent of travelling from Worcester to Edinburgh. Julia Potter, founder of J Potter Community Fitness, said: "I still can’t quite believe these numbers! "We’ve more than doubled our target, with 100 supporters contributing to the total." 100 supporters covered 776 miles in a week-long challenge (Image: J Potter Community Fitness) The event ran from October 14-21 and brought together members of the fitness community, their families, friends, and local businesses for a week of walking, fitness classes, and fundraising—all with a splash of pink. Ms Potter said the charity's work has personal meaning for her. "I lost my mum to breast cancer when she was just 56, and it’s a charity that’s incredibly close to my heart.

topic: Why Hiring the Right GM Can Be a Growth Lever for Boutique Fitness

facts.label: Story
facts.value: Why Hiring the Right GM Can Be a Growth Lever for Boutique Fitness

facts.label: Article
facts.value: Good Soul Hunting is bringing an executive search approach to one of boutique fitness’s most important roles. A fitness brand can have the strategy, concept, systems and growth plan. But members don’t experience any of those things at headquarters. They experience the brand through the studio they walk into and the people running it. That puts an enormous amount of responsibility in the hands of general managers and studio managers. They’re responsible for translating the brand’s vision into the daily experience of employees and members while also driving the performance of the business. For boutique fitness operators, hiring a GM is an operational decision with direct consequences for growth. “A great General Manager or Studio Manager isn’t just there to keep the studio running smoothly, they’re ultimately responsible for turning the brand’s vision into results at a local level,” said Matt Adey, co-founder and managing partner of Good Soul Hunting.
